In node2vec-style link prediction, the Hadamard operator and the Weighted-L2 operator are both ways to combine two node embeddings into an edge feature for a downstream classifier. On directed multi-relational knowledge graphs with typed edge predicates, the key issue is that these operators are inherently symmetric in the two endpoint embeddings, so they do not naturally encode edge direction or predicate type unless the model adds extra machinery such as separate representations for source and target roles, relation-specific features, or explicit edge-type embeddings.

As a result, their performance on such graphs is generally weaker than methods designed for directed and typed relations. The Hadamard operator often works reasonably well as a simple baseline because it preserves coordinate-wise interaction information, but it still cannot distinguish (u, v) from (v, u) by itself. The Weighted-L2 operator emphasizes coordinate-wise differences between embeddings, which can help capture dissimilarity, but it is also symmetric and therefore likewise cannot represent directionality on its own. In practice, both operators are better suited to undirected or weakly typed settings than to directed multi-relational knowledge graphs.

If you want strong performance on directed multi-relational knowledge graphs, a relation-aware model is usually preferable, for example one that learns relation-specific scoring functions or uses separate embeddings for head and tail roles. If you must use node2vec embeddings, a common workaround is to augment the edge feature with relation identity and direction indicators, rather than relying on Hadamard or Weighted-L2 alone.
